title: Setting up a street or neighbourhood composting scheme
subtitle: Organising a shared compost site for households without garden space
excerpt: A street composting scheme collects kitchen and garden waste from households that lack the space or inclination to compost individually, processes it communally, and returns the finished compost to members. The logistics are simple but the social organisation takes more thought than the bins.
sourceNotes: WRAP (Waste and Resources Action Programme) community composting guide; CAT (Centre for Alternative Technology) community resource guides; Community Composting Network UK guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A slow composting method where material is added to a heap or bin over time without active temperature management, breaking down over 6–18 months.

content.text: A street composting scheme needs a site, some bins, a small rota, and a simple agreement about what can and cannot go in. The composting itself is easy. The part that takes effort is keeping the scheme running when the original organiser goes on holiday or moves house.

A resident with a large garden who is happy to host the bins. This is the simplest arrangement. The host keeps a share of the finished compost; the responsibility for access and maintenance sits on a nominated person, not just the host.

A shared green space: an allotment site, a community garden, or a council-owned verge (needs council permission). Most councils are supportive of community composting on their land if there is a responsible contact.
The site needs to be within 200 m of the participating households — further than that and drop-off rates fall sharply. People carry a kitchen caddy, not a bin bag.
Two large bins (320-litre or 600-litre): one for active filling, one maturing. A two-bin system keeps the mature compost separate from fresh material.
A container of wood chip or cardboard torn into pieces near the bins. Participants add a handful of brown material with each caddy deposit; this is the primary quality-control step.
A printed 'what can go in' guide fixed to the bin lid. Contamination (cooked meat, oil, dairy in open
bins) causes smell and attracts rodents.
Recruit 4–8 households to start. More than 10 at launch is often harder to manage; the scheme is easier to grow than to shrink.
Agree a simple rota: one person per week checks the bins, adds brown material if needed, and flags any contamination.

Decide how the finished compost is shared — by household, by the amount deposited, or by a draw. Equality is less important than clarity; disputes about compost allocation end schemes faster than bin problems.
Set a WhatsApp group or a shared note on the bin for quick communication when something needs fixing.
What to expect in the first year

A two-bin scheme with 6 households typically produces 200–300 litres of finished compost per year. The maturation bin needs to sit for 4–6 months before harvest. The first batch is often imperfect — some coarse woody material, some unfinished kitchen waste. Screen it through a 10 mm sieve before using on beds; the oversize goes back into the active bin.

rows.cause: Too much fresh kitchen waste without brown cover; possibly cooked meat or cooked food in the bin
rows.fix: Remove any obviously wrong material; fork in a large quantity of wood chip or torn cardboard; agree to check deposits more actively for a fortnight.

rows.symptom: Participation has dropped to two households after six months
rows.cause: The scheme is not convenient enough; people default to the council food-waste bin when the scheme requires more effort
rows.fix: Move the bins closer to the drop-off point; simplify the 'what's allowed' list; consider a hot composting approach that accepts cooked food.
